 Australia Proposes Tougher Sunscreen Rules After SPF Testing Scandal 
 2026-11-01 09:00 
 Proposed Australian reforms would require sunscreen manufacturers to submit SPF test results to the national medicines regulator before products reach the market.（Photo/puhimec） 
 【 Taiwan Immigrants' Global News Network 】 /Editorial Team 
 Australia’s medicines regulator is proposing stricter sunscreen requirements following a consumer testing scandal that raised doubts about product protection claims. Testing by Australian independent consumer group Choice last year found that 16 of 20 popular sunscreens failed to deliver the SPF levels stated on their labels. One product labelled SPF 50+ recorded a result of just SPF 4, triggering a recall that was followed by 19 other products using the same base formula.
 Under the proposed reforms, manufacturers would need to conduct multiple SPF tests on finished sunscreen products and submit the results confidentially to the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) before products enter the market. Companies would also have to repeat testing periodically throughout a product’s shelf life. The regulator says the changes aim to strengthen manufacturers’ accountability and improve the reliability of sun protection claims.
 Choice has welcomed the move but argues that requiring companies to submit data is insufficient if the TGA does not routinely assess the results or make them publicly available. The group says consumers would still have limited ways to verify whether a product’s advertised protection is supported by evidence. The TGA has cited concerns over commercial confidentiality, intellectual property and the risk of technical findings being misunderstood as reasons for not publishing test results.
 The proposals also include changes to laboratory testing and accreditation. Manufacturers could use in-vitro testing, which measures sunscreen performance on a prepared surface, alongside the existing in-vivo approach involving human volunteers. The TGA says the alternative could help address inconsistencies in current testing, although it may not suit every formulation or water-resistance assessment. Stronger international accreditation for testing laboratories is also proposed. Some measures may be introduced soon, while others require further consultation or legislative changes.

 Starbucks to Relaunch Bear-Shaped Glass Cups for Holiday Season with Mystery Box Edition 
 Starbucks is bringing back its popular Bearista glass cold cups for the 2026 holiday season, adding a surprise-box version to its seasonal merchandise lineup. The return follows strong interest in the bear-shaped drinkware last year, as the coffee chain prepares to introduce a new range of festive products in the United States.The new Bearista Surprise Box Edition will go on sale at participating U.S. coffeehouses on November 10, with limited quantities available. Each box contains a mystery bear-themed glass cup, while further details about the collection are expected to be announced later. The original Bearista design will also return to selected locations from December 1, subject to availability.The distinctive glass cup features a small bear-shaped design, with its lid styled to resemble a winter hat in Starbucks’ signature green. The product is part of the company’s broader holiday merchandise collection, which typically attracts attention from customers looking for seasonal gifts and collectible items. Starbucks has not indicated that the returning cups will be available at every U.S. store.The relaunch is part of a wider holiday campaign that includes seasonal beverages and other merchandise. Starbucks plans to introduce its holiday drink menu on November 5, featuring returning favourites such as Peppermint Mocha, Caramel Brulée Latte, Sugar Cookie Latte and Gingerbread Chai. Additional holiday merchandise is scheduled for November 17, coinciding with the company’s Red Cup Day promotion.

 At Least 32 US States Move to Restrict Ultra-Processed Foods in School Meals 
 Efforts to remove ultra-processed foods from American school meals are gaining momentum, drawing support from both the Make America Healthy Again movement and progressive groups. According to The Washington Post, lawmakers in at least 32 states have proposed restricting products such as packaged snacks, sweets and processed meats in school cafeterias, citing concerns about food safety and nutrition.California and Arizona have already passed relevant laws. Arizona restricts a defined list of 11 ingredients, while California uses a broader definition that may cover foods containing certain laboratory-produced additives. California public schools must begin phasing out ultra-processed foods by July 1, 2029, with a complete ban scheduled for July 1, 2032.Some schools are already changing their menus. Santa Ana Unified School District in California began introducing scratch-cooked meals at one high school in 2021 and is now expanding the approach to its eighth campus. Nutrition services director Josh Goddard said questions from families during the COVID-19 pandemic encouraged the district to reduce reliance on prepared meals and cook more food from basic ingredients in school kitchens.Cost and kitchen capacity remain major challenges. Nutrition epidemiology researcher Lindsey Smith Taillie noted that ultra-processed products make up a substantial share of packaged foods, raising concerns about whether schools can find affordable alternatives. California schools receive about US$6 per meal and benefit from state subsidies and extensive agricultural resources, advantages that may not be available to districts elsewhere.

 Americans Warned of Detention and Exit Bans When Traveling to China 
 Americans planning trips to mainland China are being urged to take extra precautions after the U.S. State Department updated its Level 2 travel advisory, warning of potential wrongful detention, electronic surveillance and restrictions on leaving the country. The advisory highlights risks under China's broad security laws, which may classify certain professional, academic or personal activities as criminal offenses.The State Department recently issued guidance warning that emails, text messages and social media posts sent to or from China may be monitored. Officials also said some people have been detained or deported over private messages critical of Chinese authorities, including messages sent while outside the country. Those detained could face lengthy imprisonment and limited contact with family members or U.S. officials.Travelers may also encounter exit bans during investigations or business and civil disputes, even without being formally detained. Such restrictions have reportedly affected relatives of people under investigation, including children, and may remain in place for years. Some travelers might not discover the ban until they attempt to leave China, while legal avenues to challenge the restrictions may be limited.Travel expert Bobby Laurie advised visitors to minimize risks by avoiding sensitive photography, staying clear of demonstrations and carrying only essential information on their electronic devices. The State Department recommends traveling with a valid U.S. passport and Chinese visa, enrolling in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program and arranging regular check-ins with family members or employers before departure.
